hints: Think about what happens on heating a Group 2 carbonate and compare how easily $\text{MgCO}_3$ decomposes versus $\text{BaCO}_3$.
Focus on the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ion and how its size changes from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, then link this to charge density.
Consider how a small highly charging cation distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ electron cloud and weakens the C-O bonds to help form $\text{CO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Picture what thermal decomposition means**
You are heating $\text{MCO}_3$ to give $\text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$. A more stable carbonate needs a higher temperature before it breaks down. In Group 2, $\text{MgCO}_3$ decomposes easily on gentle heating while $\text{BaCO}_3$ needs very strong heating, so stability increases down the group.

Compare the cations**
All the ions are $2+$, so the difference is size. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is very small, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is much larger. Charge density is charge divided by size, so $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has high charge density and high polarising power, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ has low charge density and low polarising power.

See how the cation attacks the carbonate**
The $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion has delocalised electrons over the C-O bonds. A small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ pulls strongly on those electrons and distorts the anion. This polarisation weakens the C-O bonds and makes it easier to break off $\text{CO}_2$ to leave $\text{O}^{2-}$. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ polarises much less, so the carbonate stays intact to higher temperature.

Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2 from Mg to Ba.
Down the group cation radius increases so charge density of $\text{M}^{2+}$ decreases.
The $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion is polarised less, so C-O bonds are weakened less and decomposition is less favoured.

hints: Remember the general pattern for a metal carbonate decomposing is metal oxide plus carbon dioxide.
walkthrough:
Apply the carbonate pattern**
Just like $\text{MCO}_3 \longrightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$, copper(II) carbonate gives copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide. Copper stays as +2 on both sides, so no balancing change is needed: $\text{CuCO}_3 \longrightarrow \text{CuO} + \text{CO}_2$.

hints: Start from Cu atom $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{10} 4s^1$ and remember which electrons are lost first when forming $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Build Cu then remove electrons correctly**
Cu is unusual: $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{10} 4s^1$. When forming ions, 4s electrons are lost before 3d. So $\text{Cu}^{+}$ is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{10}$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ loses one more d electron to give $[\text{Ar}] 3d^9$. That means nine electrons spread over five 3d boxes, so four boxes are full with $\uparrow\downarrow$ and one box has a single $\uparrow$. Leave 4s and 4p completely empty.

Final answer: $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^9$: four 3d boxes contain paired electrons $\uparrow\downarrow$ and one 3d box contains one electron $\uparrow$, 4s box empty, all three 4p boxes empty.

hints: Recall that most d orbitals have four lobes, but the $d_{z^2}$ orbital is the special case with lobes on one axis plus a central ring.
walkthrough:
Visualise the $d_{z^2}$ shape**
Do not draw four clover leaves, that is $d_{xy}$ or $d_{x^2-y^2}$. For $d_{z^2}$, draw a dumbbell stretched vertically along the z-axis with a doughnut shaped torus lying flat around the centre in the xy-plane. Label the three axes x, y and z clearly.
Final answer: Sketch with two lobes centred on the z-axis (one +z, one -z) and a torus (doughnut ring) in the xy-plane, with x, y, z axes labelled.

hints: Think about the energy gap between the outer 4s level and the inner 3d level in a transition metal.
walkthrough:
Link similar energies to flexible electrons**
In transition elements the $(n+1)$s and nd levels overlap in energy. For copper the 3d and 4s are almost the same energy, so removing one electron to give +1 or two electrons to give +2 costs a similar amount of energy. That is why both oxidation states are accessible and stable in complexes.
Final answer: The 3d and 4s subshells are close or similar in energy, so variable numbers of electrons can be removed with similar energy cost.

hints: Break the word bidentate into bi meaning two, and think about what a ligand must have to bond.
Recall how any ligand bonds to a central metal ion, by donating an electron pair.
walkthrough:
Count the donor atoms**
In $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ each N has a lone pair. That gives two lone pairs per molecule available for bonding, which is the bi part of bidentate.

Name the bond type**
Each lone pair is donated into a vacant orbital on the central $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to form a dative covalent bond, also called a coordinate bond. So a bidentate ligand uses two donor atoms to make two such bonds to the same metal centre.
Final answer: Species with two lone pairs of electrons that form two dative covalent (coordinate) bonds to a central transition metal atom or ion.

hints: Remember the complex is octahedral with two monodentate $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands and two $en$ ligands that must each occupy adjacent (cis) positions.
Think where the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands can sit relative to each other, either opposite (trans) or next to each other (cis).
For the cis $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ case, consider that the two $en$ chelate rings can be arranged in two non-superimposable ways around the octahedron.
walkthrough:
Set the octahedral framework**
$\text{Cu}$ is at the centre with six positions. Each $en$ is a chelate that must span two adjacent positions, it cannot stretch across trans. The two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands fill the remaining two sites.

Draw the trans isomer**
Place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite each other, for example one up and one down. Then place one $en$ in the equatorial plane on the left and right front, and the second $en$ on the left and right back. This gives the trans form.

Draw the two cis forms**
Now place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands next to each other, for example both on the top face. There are still two ways to wrap the two $en$ ligands around the remaining four sites, mirror images in arrangement, giving cis-1 and cis-2. All three diagrams must show $en$ as an N-N bridge and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in the correct cis or trans positions.

Final answer: Three structures: one trans-$[\text{Cu(en)}_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$ with the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ opposite each other; two cis-$[\text{Cu(en)}_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$ isomers with the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ adjacent but with the $en$ ligands in different relative orientations. Each $en$ shown as N-N chelate occupying cis positions.

hints: Recall that cis-trans covers the trans versus cis $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ positions, and look for a non-superimposable mirror image pair among the cis forms.
walkthrough:
Name both stereoisomer types**
Trans versus cis $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ positions is geometrical, also called cis-trans isomerism. The two different cis arrangements are non-superimposable mirror images, which is optical isomerism.
Final answer: Optical and geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism.

hints: Compare the symmetry of the trans isomer with the cis isomers and think about whether bond dipoles cancel.
walkthrough:
Use symmetry to judge polarity**
In the trans isomer the two $\text{Cu-O}$ bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so it is non-polar. In either cis isomer the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are on the same side, the structure is asymmetric, so the individual bond dipoles add to give a net dipole and the molecule is polar.
Final answer: Either cis isomer (isomer 1 or isomer 2 with cis $\text{H}_2\text{O}$); polar bonds or dipoles do not cancel as the molecule is asymmetric.

hints: Use the formula $\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$ with $\text{Na}^+$ ions to work out the charge and composition of the negative complex.
walkthrough:
Split the salt into ions**
Three $\text{Na}^+$ give total $3+$, so to balance, the aluminium containing anion must be $3-$. It contains one Al and six F, so it is $\text{AlF}_6^{3-}$. The species bonded to Al is $\text{F}^-$, which donates a lone pair, so fluoride is the ligand.
Final answer: Complex ion is $\text{AlF}_6^{3-}$; ligand is $\text{F}^-$.

hints: Start with $Q = It$ and convert the time from minutes to seconds to get charge in coulombs.
Convert charge to moles of electrons using the Faraday constant $96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$.
Use the cathode equation $\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Al}$ to link moles of electrons to moles of Al.
Convert moles of Al to mass using $m = nM$ with $M = 27$ and give the answer to two significant figures.
walkthrough:
Calculate the charge passed**
Charge links current and time: $$Q = It$$ Time must be in seconds: $30 \text{ min} = 30 \times 60 = 1800 \text{ s}$. So $$Q = 1.5 \times 1800 = 2700 \text{ C}$$

Convert charge to moles of electrons**
One mole of electrons carries $96500 \text{ C}$: $$n(e^-) = \frac{Q}{F} = \frac{2700}{96500} = 2.80 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$$

Use the cathode stoichiometry**
From $$\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Al}$$ three moles of electrons make one mole of Al: $$n(\text{Al}) = \frac{2.80 \times 10^{-2}}{3} = 9.33 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Convert to mass to two significant figures**
$$m = nM = 9.33 \times 10^{-3} \times 27 = 0.25 \text{ g}$$ Keep two significant figures as requested, so $0.25 \text{ g}$ is the maximum mass.

Final answer: Charge $= 1.5 \times 30 \times 60 = 2700 \text{ C}$
$n(e^-) = 2700 / 96500 = 2.80 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$
$n(\text{Al}) = 2.80 \times 10^{-2} / 3 = 9.33 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
mass $= 9.33 \times 10^{-3} \times 27 = 0.25 \text{ g}$
